title: Judicial Review
lead: Judicial Review is ==sine qua non== for a federal parliamentary democracy assuring one of the world's most exhaustive sets of rights. In [[L. Chandra Kumar v. UoI (1997)]] the SC declared ==Arts 32 and 226 part of the basic structure== — though ‘judicial review’ is ==not itself mentioned== in the Constitution.

items.title: Doctrines Enhancing JR
bullets: ==Due process of law==; principles of natural justice

blocks.text: ==SC and HCs do NOT have identical JR powers.== The SC can review its own judgments via ==Review Petitions (Art 137)== and ==Curative Petitions ([[Rupa Ashok Hurra]], 2002 guidelines)==, which HCs cannot. Not all appeals are judicial review (e.g. bail-denial appeals aren't). The Constitution ==doesn't explicitly mention HC appellate jurisdiction== as it does for the SC.

sections.title: Impact on Parliamentary Democracy & Separation of Powers

head: Positive
Negative
rows: ==Policy disruption== — [[P. Chidambaram v. ED (2019)]], bail policy under scrutiny
Checks executive arbitrariness — [[Krishna Kumar (2017)]] on ordinances

items: ==Express exclusions==: CoM advice to the President/Governor (Arts 74, 163); ==legislative proceedings (Arts 122, 212)==; ==delimitation orders (Arts 329, 243O, 243ZG)==; adaptation of pre-Constitution laws by Presidential order (Art 372); ==laws added to the Ninth Schedule before 24 April 1973== (Kesavananda).

==Constitutional immunities==: ==Art 361== presidential/gubernatorial immunity for official acts; judicial immunity (Arts 124(4), 218). On the ==Ninth Schedule==, [[I.R. Coelho v. State of TN (2007)]] held laws added ==after 24 April 1973 ARE reviewable== if they violate FRs or basic structure.
==Separation of powers==: courts avoid ==‘political questions’== and the wisdom of ==policy decisions== within constitutional bounds.
==Judicial self-restraint== — e.g. the [[Supriyo]] same-sex marriage case; ==deference to expertise== of specialised bodies; ==presumption of constitutionality== with the burden on the challenger.
